title: What Are the Brazilian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget

refresh_of.note: Person: article to refresh. Check legacy slugs and other ranking pages; recommend direct 301s at publish.

notes: REFRESH: the brief reads the old page in full with mcp__Apify__apify--web-fetch; SEO pulls its ranked keywords and status and checks weddedwonderland.com for legacy slugs and other ranking pages (e.g. a Brazil destination page or a Real Weddings post). Keep its traditions if sourceable; never reuse wording; drop errors; correct brand terms.

Scope: Brazil is large and diverse; customs vary by region, faith (Catholic, Protestant and evangelical, Afro-Brazilian religions, secular) and family. Say so once; regional notes only where sourced. No stereotypes about Brazilians, no carnival cliches.

Likely customs (brief finalises): the engagement and rings worn on the right hand, moved to the left at the wedding; chá de panela (kitchen shower) and similar showers; padrinhos (wedding sponsors, often several couples); bem-casados (wedding sweets) and docinhos; the civil and religious ceremony (including religious marriage with civil effect, only if an official source says so); the bride's name written inside the dress or shoe, as often told; the groom's tie cut and sold to guests; Saint Anthony (Santo Antônio) as the matchmaking saint and the mock wedding of the Festas Juninas; music and dancing late into the night. UNESCO: Samba de Roda of the Recôncavo of Bahia (2008) and Frevo (2012) only where UNESCO's text links them to celebrations; no other UNESCO claims unless the page is confirmed live and the title matches. Portuguese spelling with diacritics.

Destination angle: Australians marrying in Brazil (Smartraveller current advice checked live, including any higher-level areas; suggest only places outside them) plus Brazilian-Australian weddings at home. Legal steps from official sources only (Brazil's civil registry, the cartório de registro civil, via gov.br or CNJ; the Australian Embassy in Brasília and Smartraveller): habilitação, certificate of no impediment, apostille, sworn translation, recognition in Australia; same-sex marriage only from an official source. 'Check with the cartório and the embassy, including any fees' where unreadable; 'a fee applies' only if an official source says so; 'as at November 2026'.

Sources: UNESCO, IPHAN (Brazil's heritage institute), gov.br, CNJ, Visit Brasil (official tourism), national museums, encyclopaedias, academic sources. Unsourced becomes 'often told' or is left out. Customs worded as 'often told' get no [[VERIFY]] marker.
Images: placeholders only; no AI images of people, cultural dress, ceremonies or places; AI only for neutral still lifes (bem-casados) labelled illustrative pending approval.

Speed: WebFetch cannot reach outside sites; Apify web-fetch (parallel) and DataForSEO from the start. Fact-check as 2 parallel batches, 15 min HARD, save after every 3 facts, separate scratch folders; no extra sourcing rounds. Google Drive disconnected; Firecrawl out of credits.
Headings must not contain pasted keywords in brackets.
Do not use 'from first idea to the last dance'; Advisor claims only from brand-facts.md (single point of contact; fee and inclusions in writing); no implied help with legal paperwork.
Person's standards: exactly 4 one-sentence Key takeaways; no prices; no vendor names; business details deferred; Australian English; no em dashes.
